title: An explanation of why spacetime has one time and three space dimensions

concept.text: Strings 2000 problem 5 (proposed by Shamit Kachru, Sunil Mukhi and Hiroshi Ooguri): why does the universe appear to have one time and three space dimensions? Sources given: https://preskill.caltech.edu/millennium.html ; https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v54.i10.14_2.online.pdf ; https://x.com/martinmbauer/status/1779906631003697211.

page.title: Dynamical origin of spacetime dimensionality and signature
page.definition: A physical theory derives why exactly three spatial dimensions are extended on observable scales and why spacetime has one time dimension. In a local orthonormal frame, the time direction has the opposite metric sign from the three spatial directions. This is Lorentzian signature. Additional microscopic spatial dimensions may remain small.

goal.need: Making six of nine spatial dimensions small can reproduce the observed count. A dynamical explanation would tell cosmologists why only three grew large and why the geometry governing causal propagation has one time direction. Those counts alone leave the particle spectrum open. One family of string compactifications yields over 170,000 inequivalent four-dimensional models resembling the Standard Model.

completion.title: An independently verified derivation selects one time and three extended spatial dimensions.
completion.criterion: A physical theory derives why observable spacetime has exactly three extended spatial dimensions and one time dimension, rather than choosing these counts as background inputs. An independent calculation verifies the dimensional and signature selection, including the physical limits of any approximation or regulator used. This is a provisional Atlas test; no field-wide numerical confidence threshold or prescribed experiment was found.
completion.set_by: Atlas provisional criterion; no external acceptance test for the combined explanation was located.
completion.basis: Searches of the Strings 2000 statement, the NORDITA numerical-quantum-gravity roadmap, dimensional-selection papers and prize criteria found no shared acceptance test for this question. The question requires an explanation of both counts. Atlas provisionally requires a joint derivation and independent verification; recovering four dimensions or three expanding matrix directions alone does not settle it.

milestones.title: A quantum-gravity model recovers effective spacetime dimension 4 at large scales.
milestones.criterion: An effective dimension measured on the model's spacetime geometries agrees with 4 at large scales. For the spectral dimension, measure how the mean probability of return to the starting point changes with diffusion time, in the large-scale regime before finite-volume effects dominate. The convention specifies no numerical tolerance.
milestones.set_by: Numerical quantum-gravity community, as summarized by Glaser and Steinhaus in section 1.3.4 of their 2019 NORDITA workshop report.
milestones.threshold_quote: whether these generalized notions of dimension agree with our expectation of four space-time dimensions on large scales.

milestones.title: A matrix-model calculation selects 3 expanding spatial directions out of 9.
milestones.criterion: In the Lorentzian type IIB matrix model, track the nine eigenvalues of the spatial extent tensor as functions of time. After a critical time, exactly three grow while the other six remain small. The eigenvalue separation tests how many spatial directions expand.
milestones.set_by: Lorentzian type IIB matrix-model literature: Kim, Nishimura and Tsuchiya (2012), subsequently examined by Aoki and colleagues (2019). This diagnostic is specific to that framework.
milestones.threshold_quote: three out of nine spatial directions start to expand at some “critical time”, after which the space has SO(3) symmetry instead of SO(9).

milestones.title: One candidate theory derives 1 time direction and 3 extended spatial directions together.
milestones.criterion: One candidate theory derives both the selection of exactly three extended spatial dimensions and the Lorentzian signature with one time dimension. Both counts must follow from the dynamics. If the derivation uses a regulator, it specifies the limit in which the selection holds.
milestones.set_by: Atlas provisional criterion; no external milestone criterion for a joint derivation of both counts was located.

milestones.title: A dynamical Wick angle selects Lorentzian signature in four spacetime dimensions.
milestones.criterion: In four dimensions, allow one entry of the local frame metric to vary as exp(iθ) for −π ≤ θ ≤ π, with the other three entries equal to +1. For massless fields at one loop with more fermionic than bosonic degrees of freedom, the Lorentzian values θ = ±π must minimize the real part of the effective potential and make its imaginary part stationary. This tests signature within that family of metrics.
milestones.set_by: Greensite's effective-potential test, also applied by Carlini and Greensite and by Odintsov, Romeo and Tucker.
milestones.threshold_quote: the real part of the effective potential is minimized (and the imaginary part is stationary) only for Lorentzian signature, and only in D=4 dimensions.

not_found: No field-wide acceptance test or prize rules for solving the combined dimensionality-and-signature question were found.
No published common milestone sequence leading to a joint explanation was found.
No statement from an academy, professional society or roadmap committee disputing the value or feasibility of the combined goal was found.
No laboratory experiment demonstrating dynamical selection of both the dimensionality and the signature of physical spacetime was found.

results.finding: Causal dynamical triangulations gave a large-scale spectral dimension of 4.02 ± 0.1 from 400 independent diffusion measurements.
results.detail: The fit excludes diffusion steps below 40, where odd and even steps give different results because of lattice discretization.
results.quote:
obtain the asymptotic value
DS(σ = ∞) = 4 .02 ± 0.1, (14)
which means that the spectral dimension extracted from the l arge-σ behaviour
(which probes the long-distance structure of spacetime) is compatible with four.

results.finding: Across four de Sitter-phase CDT parameter settings, the large-scale spectral dimension was consistent with 4.
results.detail: The large-scale values are fit extrapolations from diffusion data through 490 steps. The reported uncertainties combine statistical and systematic estimates. The authors did not estimate curvature corrections.
results.quote: We find that the long distance spectral dimension is consistent with the semiclassical dimensionality of 4

results.finding: Euclidean dynamical triangulations (3 ensembles, 4,807 sampled configurations) gave a global Hausdorff dimension of 4.1 ± 0.3.
results.detail: The full spectral dataset gives 4.08 ± 0.19 with a quadratic inverse-volume term and 3.70 ± 0.13 without it.
results.quote:
A
ﬁt designed to maximize the overlap between the curves with DH a free parameter leads to
a value DH = 4.1± 0.3, where the error is statistical only.

results.finding: Lorentzian type IIB matrix model, N = 16: 3 spatial extent eigenvalues grow after the critical time.
results.detail: N is the matrix size. The text does not report the number of Monte Carlo configurations.
results.quote:
We ﬁnd that three largest eigenvalues of
Tij(t) start to grow at the critical time tc, which suggests
that the SO(9) symmetry is spontaneously broken down
to SO(3) after tc.

results.finding: Lorentzian type IIB matrix model, N = 16: 3 spatial directions expand with one time direction fixed in the action.
results.detail: The eigenvalue split is shown at κ = 4.0. The cutoff-removal analysis takes N to infinity with κ scaled as a power of N, then sends the scaling coefficient and the spatial cutoff to infinity.
results.quote:
The SO(9)
symmetry breaks down to SO(3) at some
critical time, and the size of the three-dimensional space
increases with time.

results.finding: In the fermion-inclusive type IIB simulation (matrix size N = 16), 3 spatial extent eigenvalues grow after the critical time. The configuration count is unstated.
results.detail: The growth comes from a singular Pauli-matrix sector. In the simplified VDM model, the two dominant eigenvalues of each extended-direction spatial matrix diverge in the continuum extrapolation.
results.quote: only three out of nine directions expand after some critical time

results.finding: The fermion-inclusive type IIB simulation (matrix size N = 16) selects 3 expanding spatial directions. The configuration count is unstated.
results.detail: The continuum extrapolation applies to the simplified VDM model and retains the singular spatial structure.
results.quote: only three directions start to expand at some critical time tc.

results.finding: The one-loop massless-field calculation (no empirical sample) selects the Lorentzian Wick angle θ = ±π.
results.detail: The result uses a proper-time cutoff and assumptions about the functional integration measure.
results.quote:
For nF > nB there is only one solution, namely, D = 4
 dimensions and θ = ±π.

results.finding: The one-loop Wick-angle calculation (no empirical sample) singles out total spacetime dimension D = 4.
results.detail: The gravitational conformal mode makes the gravity contribution ill-defined as calculated. The paper conditions its conclusion on a prescription that preserves proportionality between the graviton and Klein–Gordon kinetic eigenvalues.
results.quote:
For nF > nB there is only one solution, namely, D = 4
 dimensions and θ = ±π.

results.finding: The massless one-loop Wick-angle calculation, with no sampled geometries, selects θ = ±π.
results.detail: Section 2 reproduces the earlier massless calculation and Section 4 extends it by adding a cosmological counterterm. The heat-kernel cutoff is taken to be at the Planck scale.
results.quote:
In this case, both conditions are satisﬁed at θ =±π,
which corresponds to Lorentzian signature.

results.finding: The Wick-angle theory, with no sampled geometries, permits one dynamical Wick angle under its curved-spacetime consistency conditions.
results.detail: The single-angle restriction uses tangent-space flatness, preservation of the gravitational degree count, and compatibility of the spinor covariant derivatives.
results.quote:
These conditions, taken together, also rule out having more than o ne dynamical
Wick angle in the tangent space metric, as in eq. (20).

results.finding: In 3+1-dimensional causal dynamical triangulations, a spacetime with 80,000 four-simplices reached a large-scale spectral dimension of about 4.0.
results.detail: Figure 9 uses κ₀ = 3.6 and Δ = 0.6. The measured dimension begins to fall beyond about 600 diffusion steps. The fit extrapolates to 4.43 at infinite diffusion time.
results.quote:
The spectral dimension in this case ranges from a value of about 1.8 at short scales up to a value
of about 4.0 at larger values of σ, and then starts to fall for σ greater than about 600

results.finding: Combinatorial Euclidean dynamical triangulations (2,000 configurations) give an extrapolated Hausdorff dimension of 4.21 ± 0.46.
results.detail: The Hausdorff fit uses small-distance shell-volume scaling along the critical line. The infrared spectral estimate comes from diffusion-time fits on finite lattices.
results.quote:
We find DH;∞ ¼ 4.21 /C6 0.46 which is consistent
with the emergence of four-dimensional de Sitter space in
this limit.

results.finding: The cuboid EPRL-FK spin-foam model, tested with periodic cells of up to 81 vertices, gives a large-scale spectral dimension of 4.
results.detail: With a finite upper cutoff on cell sizes, the large-diffusion-time limit gives 4. After removing that cutoff, the analytical result gives 4 in the small-α phase and depends on the assumed scaling of the Laplacian.
results.quote: For τ≫l2max, we always ﬁnd Ds = 4.

results.finding: In the deformed Lorentzian type IIB matrix model at matrix size N = 128, three of nine spatial extent eigenvalues grow rapidly at late times.
results.detail: The three-direction result used a thermalized anisotropic starting configuration. A random start gave results similar to the higher-fermion-mass run, where SO(5) remained unbroken.
results.quote: Subsequently, only three eigenvalues exhibit rapid growth.

results.finding: In Lorentzian type IIB matrix-model simulations at N = 32 with three structured initializations, exactly 3 of 9 spatial extent eigenvalues grew after a critical time.
results.detail: The complex Langevin runs used block size n = 8, fermionic mass 2, γ = 6, and ξ = 10. The fermionic mass term explicitly breaks SO(9) to SO(6) × SO(3). Random starts typically yielded six expanding directions. The large-N and zero-mass limits remain untested in this source.

results.finding: The four-dimensional massless one-loop Wick-angle potential selects θ = ±π with a fermionic excess. The calculation is analytical and has no sample size.
results.detail: Equations (4.14)–(4.15) recover the earlier result in the massless, noncompact limit. The paper also finds that small nonzero masses can shift the stationary angle away from the Lorentzian endpoints.
